items.text: Give a student access to this simulation and ask them to pour hot water on the lid.
Then, ask them to try and open the lid. The lid should come off.
Ask this: how did pouring hot water on the lid help us open it?

Record their guesses by writing them down on this screen. 

Do not agree or disagree. The next test will reveal whether they were right.

Greet students, and ask them this: what was the one thing you did today that felt super easy?

Do not agree or disagree, just listen. This is only to have a light hearted moment with the students.
Then, tell them that you are finding it difficult to do something and that you want them to try it out and see whether they find it easy.

Introduce the jar by saying it has a glass body and a steel lid.

Demonstrate how to play this simulation by trying to open the lid.
Ask if anyone would want to try. Give them access to this simulation.
It turns out that the lid is jammed! Ask some "effortless" ways to open it.

Possible way 1: Get someone stronger.

They will still have to put a lot of energy into opening. Not so effortless.

Possible way 2: Pout hot water on the lid.

Just acknowledge, but neither agree nor disagree.

Possible way 3: Put on rubber gloves or use a towel.

This could work, but it will still require lots of effort. Not so effortless.
Practice curiosity: "Let's see whether hot water can help us open the lid effortlessly."

Demonstrate how to use the instrument by measuring the lid's diameter when it is cold. 

Also, measure the glass jar's diameter when it is cold.
Give the simulation's access to a student, ask them to pour hot water on the lid, and then measure the lid's diameter. They must record an increase in the diameter.
Then, ask them to measure the diameter of the jar. They must record an increase in it too.

Proceed to "Ask/Discuss." 

After answering this, compare the answer to their guesses.

Ask this: what happened inside the lid after heating, which led to expansion?

Write down their guesses.

script.x: How did heating make it easier to open the lid?
script.a:
Initially, both the lid and the jar had the same diameter. So, there was no gap between them. They were stuck close together!

After heating, the lid's diameter grew to 7.00252, while the jar's grew to 7.00025.

So, the total gap between them after heating is (7.00252 - 7.00025)/2 = 0.001135 cm. This gap made it easier to open the lid.

items.text: Hover the magnifying glass over the lid, and ask what they see.
They might answer this: steel atoms. This is almost right. Let them know that they are seeing iron atoms.

Pour the hot water on the lid, and then hover the magnifying glass over it. 

Then, proceed to the first "Ask/Discuss." You might have to run this simulation a few many times for the students to answer the following question.

After answering, compare their guesses to the answer.
Proceed to the second "Ask/Discuss."
Reveal the key point.

items.title: Key point
items.content: When steel is heated, it expands because its atoms go far away from each other, taking up more space.

script.x: What change do you see inside the lid after heating?
script.a: The atoms are moving faster, and the distance between them has increased.

script.x: How do you explain the expansion of the lid while heating using these atoms?
script.a: The spacing between the iron atoms increased. The lid now takes up more space, which shows up as expansion.

items.text: Tell students that you have a game for them.

Start by saying that all the lids are made of steel.

Give students access to the simulation and tell them to measure lid 1's diameter when it is cold, and then pour hot water on it. 

Then, tell them to measure it again. Let students find the net expansion using the calculator in the top right corner. 

Tell them to fill the appropriate cells in the table. They must type numbers into the cells.
Repeat the same for jars 2 and 3.

Ask students to measure the largest lid when it is cold and fill the appropriate cell.

Then, ask this: If I poured hot water on it, what will its net expansion be?

Ask them to guess the exact numbers by filling the appropriate cells.

Note: the simulation does not allow one to measure the largest lid when it's hot.

Ask students to find the ratio in the fourth column for each of the jars 1, 2, and 3, and let them fill column four.

If they ask why we find this ratio, tell them to wait a bit, and they'll discover it on their own.

Now, proceed to the first "Ask/Discuss."
Proceed to the second "Ask/Discuss."
Reveal the key point.

Proceed to the third "Ask/Discuss."

Students can now use this ratio to answer this question. They must now see why the ratio is useful.

Let students do the necessary calculations and fill the appropriate cells.

items.title: Key point
items.content: Two lids that are made of steel and have the same increase in temperature will have the same ratio of net expansion to the original diameter (before heating).

items.text: Compare the result to students' guesses and see whether they were right.

Once done with the puzzle, applaud their effort and ask this: 

If we let the lids cool down to 22 degrees Celsius (from 52 degrees Celsius), will all the lids still have the same ratio of net expansion to the original diameter?
Ask them to guess, and remember what they said. Get the class to arrive at one guess (yes/no).

script.x: What is the ratio for each of the first three lids?
script.a: For each of the three lids, it is 0.00036.

script.x: What should be the ratio for jar 4?
script.a:
0.00036

Since all the lids are made of steel, and have the same increase in temperature, the pattern continues to jar 4.

script.x: What is the net expansion for lid 4?

items.text: Give students access to this simulation, and let them experiment. They must see that they all have the same ratios.
Reveal the key point.

items.title: Key point
items.content: Two lids that are made of steel and have the same decrease in temperature will have the same ratio of net contraction to the original diameter (before cooling).

items.prompt: You put the jammed jar in the freezer instead of using hot water. Does the lid come loose?
options: Yes. Cold makes the lid shrink away from the glass.
Yes. Glass shrinks more than steel.
No. Steel shrinks more than glass, so it grips tighter.
No. Cooling doesn't change anything's size.

items.prompt: A steel ball just barely squeezes through a steel ring. You put both in the oven and heat them together.
options: It still just barely squeezes through.
The ball jams in the ring.
It drops through with room to spare.
The ring snaps.

items.prompt: You shrink small enough to stand inside the steel lid as it warms up. What do you see the iron atoms doing?
options: Each atom swells up like a balloon.
New atoms squeeze into the gaps.
The atoms melt into one another.
The atoms stay the same size but sit further apart.

items.prompt: A steel bar fits perfectly between two walls that cannot move. You keep heating it, and don't stop.
options: It goes on pushing harder and harder, for ever.
It bends and bows out sideways rather than pushing any harder.
It crushes itself flat against the walls.
It quietly melts while staying perfectly straight.

items.prompt: A hot steel ring is dropped over a very long glass rod. It quickly cools and grips tight. Now heat both back up together.
options: Nothing. Both grow equally.
The ring loosens and slides off.
It grips tighter.
The shaft slides out instead
